blocks.x: I have here a fairly long article from the Long Island

Daily Press, Saturday, March 25, 1939. Obviously that other article from the newspaper called the Press is the same one, the same newspaper, Long Island Daily Press. This one is entitled "Chauncey Morehouse of Forest Hills collects Weird Drums". The subtitle is - has 14 tuned to different pitches upon which tunes can be played. And the article reads: Remember those travelogues you saw in the movies where wild savages played weird tomtoms. You saw the savages but the drums you heard were probably played in a Manhattan studio by Chauncey Morehouse of 68-41 Ingram Street, Forest Hills. Morehouse, who has played the drums for all kinds of music, has gathered a collection of exotic drums from all parts of the world. "I didn't start out to be a collector," Morehouse explained. "It was simply that I asked friends of mine who were traveling to bring back drums from various countries for me. Then at the radio studios, it was found that certain drums gave grand sound effects for drama as well as music. Now most of my drums are at sound effects studios because the sound engineers have borrowed them." Morehouse has 14 drums mounted on a semi-circular bar, each tuned to a different pitch. Tunes can be played on the drums which range through the scale from B flat to B flat, leaving one extra drum which may be tuned to any low pitch. They are known as the N'goma drums. Morehouse designed them and borrowed the name from the N'goma drum of South Africa. Actually there is no resemblance. The African

N'goma is a single drum shaped like a giant egg cup, large at the top and small at the bottom with skins on each end. The Africans dance right on the drum at tribal jam sessions, beating out the rhythm as they dance. Morehouse's drums open up a new field to the musician. The instruments do not replace ordinary ones or the tympany but represent a new musical instrument. By using different types of sticks, Morehouse achieves different effects from Boleros and Rhumbas to oriental tones. Morehouse is enthusiastic about the drums because they are melody instruments and give the player freedom for improvisation. He has played them in a film short in which he was featured with Leith Stevens and the Swing Club Orchestra. A drummer with Major Bowes on the Sunday Morning Capitol Theater Family, Morehouse has played drum specialties several times including one on his N'goma drums. Six years ago Morehouse played for a full length moving picture in which difficult sounds like the trumpeting of elephants had to be dubbed in. He found himself a sound effects man achieving all kinds of sounds including pistol shots with his drums. Morehouse was complimented for his expert rhythm. His only guide was the hands of the natives appearing in the picture. He provided the drum music for a whole series of travelogues.
